title: Micah 4:6–13
context: The LORD promises to gather the lame and scattered, make them a strong remnant, and reign over them on Mount Zion forever (4:6–7), and the former dominion will return to the daughter of Zion (4:8). Zion now cries out in distress like a woman in labor, but she will go to Babylon and be rescued there (4:9–10). Many nations gather to gloat, not knowing that the LORD has gathered them like sheaves for threshing, and Zion is called to arise and thresh (4:11–13). Versification: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14, and English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: “In that day,” says the LORD, “I will assemble that which is lame, and I will gather that which is driven away, and that which I have afflicted;
verses.arminianNotes: “In that day,” says the LORD, “I will assemble that which is lame, and I will gather that which is driven away.” Arminian readers see the LORD gathering the weak and scattered as a shepherd.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s mercy toward the afflicted. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD calls them “that which I have afflicted,” so the one who judged is also the one who restores.

verses.text: and I will make that which was lame a remnant, and that which was cast far off a strong nation: and the LORD will reign over them on Mount Zion from then on, even forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make that which was lame a remnant, and that which was cast far off a strong nation.” Arminian readers see weakness transformed into strength under the LORD’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grace making the weak a strong people. Shared ground: the LORD will reign over them on Mount Zion forever, a hope readers in both traditions commonly relate to the kingdom of God.

verses.text: You, tower of the flock, the hill of the daughter of Zion, to you it will come. Yes, the former dominion will come, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “You, tower of the flock, the hill of the daughter of Zion, to you it will come.” Arminian readers see the former dominion restored to Jerusalem, pictured as a watchtower over the flock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the promise of restored kingship. The phrase “tower of the flock” may echo Genesis 35:21, though readers in this tradition hold that connection with caution.

verses.text: Now why do you cry out aloud? Is there no king in you? Has your counselor perished, that pains have taken hold of you as of a woman in travail?
verses.arminianNotes: “Now why do you cry out aloud? Is there no king in you?” Arminian readers see Zion in distress, its leadership failing, with pains like childbirth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the present anguish of Jerusalem. Readers in this tradition note the movement in these verses between present distress and future hope, introduced by the repeated “now.”

verses.text: Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail; for now you will go out of the city, and will dwell in the field, and will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued. There the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion,” and they “will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued.” Arminian readers see exile leading to redemption.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD redeeming his people from Babylon. The mention of Babylon in Micah’s day raises dating questions, and readers in this tradition hold those questions with care while affirming the promise.

verses.text: Now many nations have assembled against you, that say, “Let her be defiled, and let our eye gloat over Zion.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Now many nations have assembled against you, that say, ‘Let her be defiled, and let our eye gloat over Zion.’” Arminian readers see hostile nations gathering to gloat over Zion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the nations’ hostility. Readers in this tradition note that the nations see only an opportunity, while the next verse reveals the LORD’s hidden purpose.

verses.text: But they don’t know the thoughts of the LORD, neither do they understand his counsel; for he has gathered them like the sheaves to the threshing floor.
verses.arminianNotes: “But they don’t know the thoughts of the LORD, neither do they understand his counsel; for he has gathered them like the sheaves to the threshing floor.” Arminian readers see God turning the nations’ plans to his purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s counsel hidden from the nations. On God using hostile nations without being the author of their sin, readers may consult the existing Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horn iron, and I will make your hoofs bronze. You will beat in pieces many peoples. I will devote their gain to the LORD, and their substance to the Lord of the whole earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horn iron, and I will make your hoofs bronze.” Arminian readers see Zion strengthened by the LORD to overcome its enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal: the gathered nations are threshed. Shared ground: their gain is devoted to “the Lord of the whole earth,” so the victory belongs to God rather than to Zion’s own might.
